title: private-deploy-vpc-dns-tls-egress-debug-notes
content:
Summary:
- Customer private deployment intermittently fails to reach Redwood control-plane endpoints from customer VPC. Failures show up as: API timeouts from the runtime container, TLS handshake failures when calling control plane, and occasional successful calls after reboots.
- Affects both control-plane registration and periodic telemetry (heartbeat) egress. Not affecting local model inference (local-only).
- Hypothesis space: VPC peering route misconfig + DNS resolving to inaccessible IPs + TLS SNI/ALPN mismatch for peered connectivity + egress NAT capacity/security group issue.

Timeline & observable symptoms:
- 2026-02-18 10:12 UTC: First alert from customer: runtime container logs show repeated "timeout connecting to control-plane.redwood.com:443".
- 2026-02-18 10:18 UTC: SRE observed occasional successful heartbeats after container restart.
- 2026-02-19: Attempted several restarts, no consistent fix.

Commands tried and outputs (raw-ish fragments):
1) DNS checks from host (k8s node) and from runtime container:
- kubectl exec -it runtime-0 -- nslookup control-plane.redwood.com
  Server: 10.0.0.2
  Address: 10.0.0.2#53
  Name: control-plane.redwood.com
  Address: 172.31.45.21
  
  Note: IP above is in customer VPC CIDR (172.31.0.0/16). Expected: should resolve to peered-control-plane IP (172.31.45.21) — OK for peering.

- kubectl exec -it runtime-0 -- dig +short control-plane.redwood.com
  172.31.45.21

Observation: DNS consistently resolves to 172.31.45.21 from container.

2) Connectivity/TCP low-level checks:
- curl -vI https://172.31.45.21:443 --connect-timeout 5
  * About to connect() to 172.31.45.21 port 443 (#0)
  * Trying 172.31.45.21...
  * connect to 172.31.45.21 port 443 failed: Connection timed out
  * Failed to connect to 172.31.45.21 port 443: Connection timed out

- traceroute -n 172.31.45.21
  1  10.0.1.1  1.0 ms  0.9 ms  1.0 ms
  2  10.2.4.5  2.1 ms  2.0 ms  2.2 ms
  3  * * *
  (stops after internal hop)

Interpretation: packets not reaching destination; likely route table or ACL drop.

3) TLS handshake probe (openssl):
- openssl s_client -connect control-plane.redwood.com:443 -servername control-plane.redwood.com -brief -timeout 5
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  1400...error:1408F10B:SSL routines:SSL3_GET_RECORD:wrong version number
  no peer certificate
  ---
  
  Intermittent; sometimes returns handshake but with cipher mismatch; most often timeout.

4) EC2/VPC-level checks (customer account, run by customer):
- aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc" --query 'RouteTables[*].Routes'
  Routes show: local for 172.31.0.0/16, route for 10.2.0.0/16 -> pcx-07 (peering), no explicit route for Redwood control plane subnet 172.31.45.0/24 passing through NAT.

- Customer forwarded: "There's a redundant NAT gateway in a different AZ with a limited route table; some subnets were missing the peering route."

5) iptables and host firewall checks on node (from node):
- sudo iptables -L -n | grep 172.31.45.21  --> no matches
- sudo ufw status verbose  --> inactive

6) tcpdump captures (30s) on node interface while triggering curl:
- tcpdump -n host 172.31.45.21 and port 443 -c 100
  No packets observed leaving the node when curl times out. When curl succeeds (rare), packets present and reply from 172.31.45.21 ~30ms.

Working theory so far:
- DNS resolves to an internal IP in customer VPC (expected due to peering + private endpoint). However, route propagation is inconsistent across subnets/nodes causing some nodes to have no path to that IP. This explains intermittent success after container restarts (traffic may get routed via a node that has a correct route).
- The TLS oddities are likely noise from hitting an unexpected intermediate (e.g., a load balancer listening on TLS but with stricter TLS versions) when peering routed to wrong path — but must still rule out hostname/SNI mismatch.
- Another possibility: if traffic is forced out via NAT gateway and then back in (hairpin), security groups or NACLs block return traffic; but tcpdump shows no outbound packets when failing, pointing upstream of node (i.e., node doesn't send packets).

Next diagnostic steps attempted / planned:
- Ask customer to run route table check across ALL subnets (not just primary) and confirm route to pcx-07 for the runtime subnets. (done, found two subnets missing the route)
- Confirm VPC peering connection status (aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections) - status "active" but route table associations incomplete.
- Reproduce from different node in cluster: results vary — nodes in subnets with missing route always fail.
- Suggest quick mitigation: add explicit route in those subnets to pcx-07 (customer did, provisional) and monitor.
- Validate after route patched: connectivity restored across all nodes in tests (2026-02-21 09:40 UTC).

Notes on TLS and DNS:
- Need to ensure control-plane.redwood.com SNI is sent (openssl s_client used -servername). runtime client uses standard HTTPS libs (Go net/http) which sends SNI. Should be fine.
- If customer uses internal load balancer IPs that host multiple services, SNI required. Verify ALB/NLB listener configs on our side for peered traffic (action: infra team to check listener certs and ALPN).

Post-mortem (draft):
- Root cause: Incomplete route table propagation for VPC peering in a subset of customer private subnets. Result: nodes in those subnets could not reach control-plane private IP, causing TLS timeouts and intermittent success when traffic was scheduled on nodes with correct routing.
- Contributing factors: customer terraform/automation only associated routes with a subset of private subnets; lack of a validation check on our onboarding that verifies connectivity from each runtime subnet (we only tested from one bootstrap host).
- Remediation taken: customer added missing route entries to route tables for affected subnets (2026-02-21). Infra validated connectivity from multiple nodes.
- Follow-ups: 1) Add a preflight connectivity test during Private deployment onboarding that verifies DNS resolution and TCP handshake to control-plane from at least 3 randomly selected nodes across subnets; 2) Add docs checklist for customer infra (route table assoc, security groups, NACLs, NAT hairpin scenarios); 3) Instrument control-plane to return clearer TLS handshake logs for private-peered sources (enable access logging on ALB); 4) Update runbook for SRE on diagnosing peering route errors.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Did we see any connection attempts that reached a wrong LB (i.e., an external IP) that would explain the SSL version error? Need infra to crosscheck ALB logs (access logs) for times of failure.
- Should we add an onboarding step that verifies route tables via IAM role we provide to customers (read-only)? Pros/cons: easier verification vs. security concerns.
- Revisit runtime back-off/retry policy: add jitter and longer retry window for registration attempts so short routing churn doesn't cause repeated token failures.

Appendix — useful commands for customers / runbook snippets:
- Verify DNS from host/container:
  dig +short control-plane.redwood.com
  nslookup control-plane.redwood.com 10.0.0.2

- Check TCP reachability quickly:
  curl -vI --connect-timeout 5 https://control-plane.redwood.com:443 || true
  openssl s_client -connect control-plane.redwood.com:443 -servername control-plane.redwood.com -brief -timeout 5 || true

- Route table quick check (aws):
  aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>" --query 'RouteTables[*].{Id:RouteTableId,Associations:Associations,Routes:Routes}' --output json
  # look for route to pcx-<id> for runtime subnets

- Quick tcpdump to see if node emits packets:
  sudo tcpdump -n host <control-plane-ip> and port 443 -c 100 -w /tmp/pcap.pcap

Notes to self: capture logs for 2026-02-18 10:12 - 10:40 window and push to S3 for infra team. Follow up with Mira (mira-singh) to request ALB access logs around those timestamps.

Last checked: 2026-02-25 by rachel-lee.
